questions.question: Distinguish economic growth from economic development, explain how each is measured, and describe how the two can part company in both directions.
questions.expected_answer: Economic growth is the increase in a country's output of goods and services, measured as the annual percentage change in real GDP — real so inflation cannot masquerade as progress — and it must be read against population growth: real growth below the population growth rate (around one and a half percent a year) means the average person is becoming poorer despite a growing economy. Economic development is the broader rise in a population's quality of life: income plus health, education, housing, safety and widening real choices, measured by indicators such as life expectancy, infant mortality, literacy and access to services, and by the composite Human Development Index averaging three dimensions — a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living. The two usually travel together, since growth funds clinics and classrooms, but can separate: growth without development occurs when capital-intensive mineral-export growth lifts GDP while employment, schooling and life expectancy stand still (the enclave pattern, visible in South Africa's history of growth alongside exclusion); development without growth occurs when grants, housing, treatment and schooling programmes lift social indicators through weak-growth years, as in South Africa's post-2004 record. Every data set should therefore be asked both questions.

questions.question: Set out the demand-side and supply-side approaches to raising growth and development, and evaluate them against each other in the South African context.
questions.expected_answer: Demand-side approaches raise spending — expansionary fiscal policy (infrastructure, public employment, grants to poorer households whose high propensity to consume powers the multiplier), expansionary monetary policy (lower interest rates and easier credit), and courted export demand. With mass unemployment implying spare capacity, stimulus should raise output and jobs, and grants visibly cut poverty now. But four walls limit it: inflation (if constraints are supply-side, spending lifts prices and the central bank's higher rates cancel the stimulus); imports (a high marginal propensity to import leaks stimulus abroad — the small multiplier); debt (borrowing crowds social spending as interest costs grow and lenders price risk); and structure (spending cannot create untrained skills or unmaintained ports). Supply-side approaches expand productive capacity: the cost environment (power, transport, communications, less red tape), human capital (schooling, colleges, health), natural and physical capital (investment incentives, R&D, technology), efficient markets (competition policy, labour matching, small-business finance) and incentives (production-rewarding taxes, policy certainty). Only capacity growth is durable and it targets the actual binding constraints — but it is slow, can be regressive in the short run, and depends on state capacity. The mature evaluation is sequencing and proportion: demand-side measures carry people through the present; supply-side measures decide whether the future outgrows it — do both in proportion, softening the swings while raising the trend.

questions.question: Outline South Africa's post-1994 growth strategies with a fair verdict on the record, and explain the north-south divide — its contrasts, the mechanisms holding it open, and the counter-currents.
questions.expected_answer: The procession: RDP (1994) led with basic needs — housing, water, electrification — demand-side in spirit; GEAR (1996) swung supply-side — fiscal discipline, deficit cuts, trade opening, investor confidence — steadying the budget while growth and jobs undershot; ASGISA (2006) targeted binding constraints — infrastructure and skills; the NDP (2012) aims at 2030 — poverty eliminated and inequality cut through infrastructure, education, a capable state and faster growth. Verdict with both hands: macroeconomic stability was achieved and defended, and the social wage (grants, housing, water, electrification, public healthcare) is a genuine development gain; but growth has trailed population for over a decade, unemployment is among the world's highest, and the constraints every plan named — electricity, logistics, skills, state capacity — remain. The north-south divide: the developed north (North America, Western Europe, Japan, Australia) holds a minority of world population but most income, technology and financial power; it exports manufactures, services and capital and writes the rules in institutions where its votes weigh most. The south exports volatile primary commodities, owes debt in currencies it cannot print, receives conditional aid and loses skills to emigration. Gap-keeping mechanisms: deteriorating terms of trade, debt service consuming development budgets, tariff escalation taxing processed goods more than raw ones, and the brain drain. Counter-currents: the rise of China, India and Brazil, south-south trade and BRICS, the AfCFTA building southern scale, and remittances rivalling aid. South Africa straddles the divide — northern in finance, universities and industry; southern in poverty, inequality and unemployment.
